verdict: The idiomatic core here is genuinely good and genuinely Brazilian: tô com + noun, me vê, a gente with a singular verb, the você-form imperative, tem for there is, dele over seu, ir + infinitive for the future, and the honest notes on tá, né, pra and the -inho softener. Three structural problems undercut it. First, the list has been merged from two passes and never de-duplicated: I counted more than eighty repeated headwords, often with contradictory tiers on the same word (cozinhar appears three times at tiers 3, 2 and 3; pra mim, olha, ficar and na frente de three times each; the Dona/Seu address item five times; que horas são? at tier 1 and tier 2), which means the spaced-repetition schedule will teach the same card as if it were new and the tier ordering is not internally consistent. Second, the Hindi spine still shows through: sal, batata, leite, salada, mamãe, menino and the noun ajuda sit at tier 1 on the strength of namak, aloo and madad rather than anything a Brazilian day requires, while thirteen dead N/A slots (three of them saying the same thing about tia) occupy real estate, and one of them, hs-0245, is simply wrong because os senhores / as senhoras is precisely the honorific plural it declares nonexistent. Third, and most serious, walking the learner's day exposes holes a Brazilian-first curriculum would never have: he cannot say comer, querer, tomar, achar, conseguir or perder; he cannot name a cerveja, a praia, a padaria, a restaurante or his own endereço; he cannot ask cadê, dá pra, or quantos anos você tem; he cannot shout socorro or report a theft; boa tarde exists only inside other items' notes; and there is not one line of pronunciation guidance anywhere, which for a British ear facing 'si-DA-dji', 'bra-ZIU' and 'HOO-a' is the difference between a course that works and one that does not. Alongside those, fix the scattered factual errors flagged above, chiefly the claim that meia means 30, the blanket ban on 'pra eu' (correct before an infinitive), the sexta pronunciation note, and the outdated preto/negro framing, and repair the roman field, which silently drops diacritics from hs-0787 onward and so renders é as e, às as as and tô as to in learner-facing text.

'ainda não' = not yet
The great Brazilian filler: 'tipo assim...'. Also 'que tipo de?' = what kind of?

items.word: aqui – aí – lá / este – esse – aquele / isto – isso – aquilo
items.roman: aqui - ai - la / este - esse - aquele / isto - isso - aquilo
items.en: the three-way distance grid: by me – by you – over there
items.note: Spoken Brazilian collapses este into esse; 'aí' means 'there by you' and powers 'e aí?' = so?/alright?
'lá na frente' = up ahead
'entre' = between two things
In speech just use 'pra': 'vai pra praia'
'lá em casa' = at mine/round ours; 'na casa dele'
'menos de' before a number: menos de dez reais
'vai agora, senão perde o ônibus'
'nem a pau' is the slangier version
'parece que vai chover'
Short for 'Nossa Senhora'. Fits surprise, dismay and admiration alike
Casual. 'Muito obrigado' is standard – 'obrigada' if you're female
Casual and blokey. 'Desculpa' is the everyday standard
'Olha só' = check this out / here's the thing
Comes after: 'tá caro demais'. On its own it means brilliant: 'foi demais!'
'todo o dia' = the whole day, but 'todo dia' = every day
The spoken default; 'muitos' sounds bookish next to it
'ficou caro', 'ficou bravo'. 'virar' = to turn into; 'tornar-se' is formal. ficar also = to stay
'ter que' + infinitive is the everyday 'must'
'pelo jeito ele não vem'
'tô me arrumando'; 'tá pronto?' = are you ready?
Standard sign-off. 'a gente' = we, with third-person singular verbs
'tô chegando' = I'm nearly there (frequently untrue)

items.en: to come back, to go back
items.note: 'já volto' = back in a minute

items.en: go (in order) to do: vou almoçar, saí pra correr
items.note: 'ir' + infinitive is also how Brazilians say the future: 'vou fazer' beats 'farei'
'chuva' = rain; 'garoa' = drizzle; 'temporal' = a downpour
'fazer uma reserva'; for a cab you 'pedir um Uber'

items.en: to answer the phone; to serve a customer
items.note: 'ninguém atendeu' = nobody picked up
'passa pra sua mãe'
'chamar um Uber'; 99 is the local rival; street taxis still exist
Only São Paulo, Rio, Brasília and a few others have one
Mostly historic now the apps quote a fixed fare
Same form for a man or a woman: 'o/a motorista'
mochila = backpack, sacola = carrier bag, mala = suitcase
'tá um trânsito' = the traffic's awful; 'engarrafamento' is the formal word
'na fila'; there's a priority queue (fila preferencial) for the elderly and pregnant
'dá pra ir a pé?' = is it walkable?
'fica longe daqui?'; 'é pertinho' = it's just there
Trains barely exist outside São Paulo and Rio; it's buses and flights that run late

items.en: which platform does it go from?
items.note: At the coach station (rodoviária) the word is plataforma
'esse lugar tá ocupado?' = is this seat taken?
'tô indo' does the same job
'qual o preço?'; 'quanto custa?' is just as common
'no dinheiro ou no cartão?'; 'em espécie' is the formal term
Universal in Brazil, free and instant: 'faz um Pix pra mim', 'aceita Pix?'
Also means a bench – and the cash machine is 'o caixa eletrônico'
Haggling belongs to markets (feiras) and street stalls, not shops
The -inho does the softening; said with a smile
'trocado' = loose change; 'troco' = the change you're given back
'cel' in writing; 'meu número' for your number
'grupo da família' – you will be added to one
'chamada de vídeo' = video call
Also the drum section of a samba school
'tô sem sinal' = I've got no reception
'app' in speech too; 'baixar o app' = download the app
Pronounced 'on-lain'; 'tá online' = they're online
'não tô te vendo / não tô te ouvindo' for the other cases
'te ligo' – object pronoun before the verb, as always in Brazil
'o ar' is short for ar-condicionado; 'liga o ventilador' for the fan
Strongest in Minas and the Northeast; 'caramba!' works everywhere
'que isso!' does the same job in one breath
The standard consolation, often 'acontece, né'
'tô aqui à toa' = I'm just hanging about. 'nada não' brushes off a question
Agreement, sign-off and greeting ('beleza?') all in one word
'achar' also = to think: 'acho que sim'

items.en: greet with a kiss on each cheek
items.note: Women greet everyone this way, men hug or shake hands. Two kisses in Rio, one in São Paulo, three in some places
'missa' = mass; evangelical churches are everywhere too
'ficar chateado' = to get upset; 'tá puto' is much stronger and rude
'tô com medo' = I'm scared; 'medo de' + noun
'dar risada' is the everyday phrase; 'kkkk' is Brazilian for 'haha' in messages
'trocar' = to swap or exchange (trocar de roupa, trocar dinheiro); 'mudar de casa' = to move house
'deixa quieto' is the same idea
One word for both; 'cantar' = to sing
Also a filler while you think, and a shrug at an unanswerable question
With Uber/99 the fare is fixed in the app; in a street taxi ask for the taxímetro

items.word: primeiro, segundo, terceiro, quarto, quinto, sexto…
items.roman: primeiro, segundo, terceiro, quarto, quinto, sexto...
items.en: ordinals; all agree for gender (primeira, segunda)
items.note: Past 10th, spoken Brazilian just uses cardinals: 'andar treze', 'página vinte'
'faltam dez pras nove' – or simply 'oito e cinquenta'
'farol' in São Paulo, 'sinal' in Rio, 'semáforo' on signs. 'sinal' also = phone reception
192 for SAMU (ambulance), 190 for the police, 193 fire
'pedir no iFood' = order a takeaway; 'pedir a conta' = ask for the bill
'vira à direita', 'dobra a esquina'. virar also = to turn into something
With movement verbs speech uses 'aonde': 'aonde você vai?'
'quebra o galho' = it'll do the job; 'serve' = that'll do
Usually 'fazer o quê, né' with a shrug
Signs and instructions only – speech uses 'usar' (hs-1151)
Reading numbers aloud, Brazilians say 'meia' (half a dozen) for 6 to avoid confusion with 'três'
'cem' on its own, but 'cento e ...' whenever something follows
Same word as 'bedroom'; feminine quarta
'pras' = para as. 'cinco e quarenta e cinco' is just as common
'no fim de semana'; 'feriadão' = a long bank-holiday weekend

items.word: primeiro de maio, dois de maio, quinze de agosto…
items.roman: primeiro de maio, dois de maio, quinze de agosto...
items.en: dates: ordinal only for the 1st, plain cardinals after
items.note: Same rule as Hindi. Written 15/08 – day first, like Britain
Months are lower-case in Portuguese
Carnaval usually falls here
Festas juninas month – the winter festival season
The everyday way to say it; 'esposa' is more formal. 'meu marido' = my husband
'noivo/noiva' = fiancé(e), and also groom/bride on the day
The polite term (fila preferencial para idosos); 'terceira idade' in officialese
'velhinho' softens it; of people prefer 'idoso'. 'meu velho' = my old man
Now the standard arrangement; 'empregada' (live-in maid) is the older, loaded term
'osso duro de roer' = a tough nut to crack
'café amargo' = coffee without sugar
'experimenta!' = go on, try it. Also 'provar' a garment in the changing room
At the market you buy by weight: 'me vê meio quilo de tomate'
Runs off a gas bottle (botijão) that you order by phone
'sacolinha' for the thin plastic ones; many shops charge for them now
The cheap way to survive the heat: 'liga o ventilador'

items.en: electric shower (heats the water at the head)
items.note: How most Brazilian homes get hot water; there's no boiler
'tô suando' = I'm sweating
'descer' = to go down, and it's also how you get off a bus: 'vou descer aqui'
Said to everyone – the lift, the doorman, the bus driver. Skipping it reads as rude
Both the greeting after dark and the farewell. 'Boa tarde' from noon till sundown
The universal Brazilian hospitality offer; refusing twice is polite, refusing three times is odd
Same words as 'how long' (hs-0988) but as an exclamation on meeting or ringing
'fica tranquilo' and 'deixa disso' do the same work
'saudade' is the noun – 'saudade de você', 'que saudade!'. Brazilians say it freely to friends and family
'tô numa correria' = I'm run off my feet. Also 'occupied' of a seat or a loo
'tô de boa' = I'm free and easy; 'de graça' = free of charge
'trabalho' = work. Small talk opener: 'no que você trabalha?'
'como vão os estudos?' asked of any young relative; 'estudar' = to study
'tô na facul'; 'universidade' is the formal word, 'escola' = school
The evening fixture in Brazilian homes and a constant topic of conversation
'o jogo do Flamengo'; 'partida' is formal; 'torcer pro...' = to support
'o Jornal Nacional' is the evening bulletin; 'notícia' = a news item
'pronto-socorro' (PS) is A&E, and where you'd actually be taken; UPA for urgent care
'dor no joelho'
'segura aí' = hold this / hang on. 'pegar' = to grab, take, catch
'o celular caiu'; 'caiu a ligação' = the call dropped; 'caiu a internet' = the wifi's gone
Portuguese has no feed/give-a-drink causative pair: 'oferecer um cafezinho', 'dar água pro cachorro'
'ninguém' = nobody. In questions alguém covers 'anyone': 'tem alguém aí?'
'ele deve estar em casa', 'deve ser caro' – the everyday way to guess

items.en: about to: I'm just leaving / I was about to ring you
items.note: 'tô saindo' = I'm on my way out; 'tava pra te ligar' = I was about to call. 'estar prestes a' is written-only
'faz direito', 'come direito'. Careful: 'direita' = right-hand side
Your host will insist. 'Tô satisfeito, obrigado' declines politely – 'tô cheio' is blunt

items.en: let me know when you get there
items.note: The standard send-off; 'manda mensagem quando chegar' is the same
'mandou bem' = you did well; 'parabéns' = congratulations
'que fofo!' for children, pets and presents; 'lindo' = lovely, beautiful
Havaianas are the national footwear – worn to the shop, not to the office
Five days in Feb/March when the country stops; 'festa junina' in June is the other big one
'RG' is the Brazilian ID card people are asked for instead
The everyday verb; 'utilizar' (hs-1085) is formal. Also 'to wear': 'usar óculos'
'áudio' = the voice note everyone sends instead of typing
'aniversário' on its own always means birthday
Always plural: 'meus óculos'. 'óculos de sol' = sunglasses
como, come, a gente come, comem. The verb is used in eight notes across the list but never taught. 'comer fora' = to eat out.
quero, quer, querem. 'quer um café?' is the standard offer, 'quer que eu ajude?' the standard help. Never appears as a headword despite driving six chunks.

items.en: to have; to take; to drink
items.note: the verb beber only half covers: tomar café, tomar uma cerveja, tomar remédio, tomar banho, tomar um Uber, tomar cuidado.
from midday until dark, then boa noite. Said to the doorman, the driver and the whole lift. Only bom dia and boa noite have entries.

de/te before i or at the end = 'dji/tchi'; final -l = 'u'; r- and -rr- = an English h; final -r of infinitives usually drops (falar = 'fa-LÁ'). The single biggest listening barrier for a British ear, and the list has no pronunciation content at all.
ordered as a big shared bottle to pour into small glasses. 'uma cerveja bem gelada'; 'breja' is the slang.
mar = sea, areia = sand, quiosque = the beach bar, barraca = the stall with the chairs. It appears twice inside example sentences and never as a word.
lanchonete = the snack bar, boteco = the corner bar, churrascaria = the grilled meat place.
bakery, café and corner shop in one, open from six. Where the pão francês and the cafezinho come from. Referenced in four notes, never taught.
'qual é o endereço?' – you type it into the app or read it to a driver. Format: Rua X, 123, and then the bairro (neighbourhood).

items.en: to manage; to be able to
items.note: consigo, consegue. 'não consegui' = I couldn't do it; 'consegue me ajudar?' softer than 'pode'. One of the commonest spoken verbs and it is absent.
both jobs: acho que sim, achei o hotel. Three chunks in the list depend on it (eu acho que, achei!, o que você achou?) but the verb is never introduced.
'cadê o banheiro?', 'cadê você?'. No verb needed, and it beats 'onde está' in speech. Currently only mentioned inside two notes.

items.en: is it possible to ...? / can't be done
items.note: 'dá pra ir a pé?' = is it walkable; 'dá pra pagar no cartão?'; 'não dá' is the standard soft refusal you will be given.
the emergency shout, buried in a note at present. 190 police, 192 ambulance (SAMU), 193 fire.
irregular comparative of bom, so 'mais bom' is wrong: tá melhor, é melhor a gente ir, o melhor de todos. pior = worse.
'que legal!' = brilliant, 'tá legal' = fine by me, 'ele é muito legal' = he's lovely. maneiro, bacana and massa are the regional swaps.
perdi a chave, perdi o ônibus, 'tô perdido' = I'm lost. Only the form perdi appears, inside a note.
answered with ter, never ser: 'tenho quarenta anos'. Basic small talk and it is missing entirely.
'onde fica o ponto?'. You put your arm out or the bus goes straight past.

items.word: pra viagem ou pra comer aqui?
items.roman: pra viagem ou pra comer aqui?
items.note: the counter question at every lanchonete and padaria. Answer with 'pra viagem' or 'pra comer aqui'.

items.word: cê vai? / tá bom / pra onde / brigado
items.roman: cê vai? / tá bom / pra onde / brigado
items.en: spoken reductions: hear them, you needn't say them
items.note: você = cê, está = tá, para = pra, para o = pro, obrigado = brigado, para a = pra. Spoken Brazilian runs a fifth shorter than the written line, which is why a textbook-trained ear stalls.
cachaça, lime and sugar, muddled at the table. 'de vodca' makes it a caipiroska; 'com pouco açúcar' if you want it drier.
served in small glasses, very cold, with a head. 'mais um chope' keeps the table going.
'passar protetor'; strength is 'fator 50'. The equatorial sun catches a British complexion inside an hour.
against the dengue mosquito, sold in every farmácia. 'pernilongo' and 'muriçoca' are the mosquito itself.
'é perigoso ali?' is a normal thing to ask a local about a street or a time of night, and you get a straight answer.
said in the plural with no subject, as English uses the passive. 'fui assaltado' = I was mugged; delegacia = the police station where you file the boletim de ocorrência.
PUXE looks like push and means pull. Also on signs: entrada, saída, caixa, elevador.

items.en: do you want your tax number on the receipt?
items.note: asked at practically every till after 'débito ou crédito?'. As a visitor you have no CPF, so the answer is 'não, obrigado'.
what counter and shop staff open with, despite the não. Recognise it and answer; you never need to produce it.
'nem eu' = me neither, 'nem sempre' = not always, 'nem sei' = I've no idea. High frequency and completely absent.

items.en: to find a way round it
items.note: 'a gente dá um jeito' is a promise that it will be sorted somehow. The jeitinho is a national self-description, half proud and half rueful.
o shopping = the mall, notebook = a laptop, outdoor = a billboard, smoking = a dinner jacket, office boy = a runner. Said with Portuguese vowels, so they are harder to catch than real Portuguese.
